title: Cooling the City
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On a still summer night, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. The effect was first described in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur meteorologist who compared temperature readings taken in London with those from villages outside it, and it is now known as the urban heat island. For most of the two centuries since, it was regarded as little more than a curiosity. As heatwaves become more frequent and more of the world's population moves into cities, it is increasingly treated as a threat to public health. The elderly, young children and people with heart or lung conditions are especially vulnerable, because the body's natural means of cooling itself depends on cooler nights in which to recover from hot days.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The causes are well understood. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofing felt absorb most of the sunlight that falls on them and release it slowly as heat after sunset, which is why the difference between city and countryside is usually greatest at night. Tall buildings on either side of narrow streets trap this heat and block the breezes that might carry it away. Cities also lack vegetation, which cools the air as water evaporates from leaves, and they generate heat of their own from vehicles, industry and, ironically, from air conditioners, which cool the inside of a building by warming the street outside.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The simplest remedy is to change the colour of the city. A white roof reflects most of the sun's energy back into the sky, and on a hot afternoon its surface may be thirty degrees cooler than that of a black roof beside it. The paint is cheap, and applying it requires no special skill. New York began a programme of coating flat roofs with white paint in 2009, using volunteers to do much of the work. The benefit is felt chiefly by the people living on the top floor, whose need for air conditioning falls; the effect on the temperature of the street below is much smaller. In cold climates there is also a penalty, since a reflective roof absorbs less of the sun's warmth in winter and heating bills may rise slightly.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Roads cover an even larger share of a city than roofs, and Los Angeles has experimented with painting streets a pale grey. Measurements confirmed that the treated surfaces were considerably cooler to the touch. The results for people, however, were less encouraging. Researchers who walked the streets with instruments found that sunlight bouncing off the pale surface struck pedestrians from below, so that a person standing on the road at midday could actually feel hotter than before. The coating also wore away under traffic and needed to be reapplied. Reflective paving, it appears, is better suited to places where few people walk, such as car parks.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Trees suffer from neither drawback. They cast shade on pavements and walls, and they cool the surrounding air through evaporation. The Colombian city of Medellín has planted thousands of trees and shrubs along roads and waterways to form what it calls green corridors, and reports that temperatures along them have fallen by around two degrees. But trees are slow. A sapling may take twenty years to provide useful shade, and during that time it must be watered and protected, an expense that city budgets frequently overlook. Trees are also unevenly shared. In many cities, surveys have shown that wealthy districts have far more tree cover than poor ones, with the result that those least able to afford air conditioning live in the hottest streets.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some cities have concluded that, while they wait for the trees to grow, the priority must be to protect the people most at risk. After a heatwave in 2010 that was blamed for more than a thousand deaths, the Indian city of Ahmedabad drew up a plan under which hospitals are warned in advance of dangerous temperatures, public buildings are opened as places to cool down, and outdoor labourers are advised to change their working hours. The plan cost little and has been widely copied. Its lesson is that the heat island is not only a problem of materials and design. Who suffers in a hot city depends as much on how that city is organised as on how it is built.

groups.instruction:
Reading Passage 2 has six paragraphs, A–F.
Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below.
groups.limit: Write the correct number, i–ix, next to Questions 14–19.

options.i: Why cities hold on to heat
options.iii: The rising cost of air conditioning
options.iv: A measure that mainly benefits those directly beneath it
options.v: Protecting residents through organisation rather than construction
options.vi: An old observation that has gained new importance
options.vii: A comparison of city temperatures in different countries
options.viii: A slow remedy that is not shared equally
options.ix: How wind speeds vary from one city to another

groups.instruction:
Look at the following statements (Questions 20–23) and the list of measures below.
Match each statement with the correct measure, A, B, C or D.
groups.limit:
Write the correct letter, A, B, C or D, next to Questions 20–23.
NB You may use any letter more than once.

items.text: It may make people who are outdoors feel warmer.
It can lead to slightly higher energy costs at one time of year.
It needs continuing care for many years before it becomes effective.
It has to be renewed because vehicles damage it.

groups.limit: Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

rows.text: Luke Howard compared temperatures recorded in London with those recorded in {24} outside the city.
Vegetation cools the air when water evaporates from {25}.
Under the Ahmedabad plan, {26} receive early warning of dangerous temperatures.

questions.explain:
答案是 vi。A 段說熱島效應早在十九世紀初就被 Luke Howard 描述過，兩百年來只被當成 a curiosity，現在則 increasingly treated as a threat to public health。
同義轉換：first described in the early nineteenth century ＝ an old observation；increasingly treated as a threat ＝ gained new importance。
questions.quote: it is increasingly treated as a threat to public health

questions.explain:
答案是 i。B 段第一句 The causes are well understood，接著列出成因：深色表面吸熱、高樓困住熱、缺乏植物、城市自己產生熱。
陷阱：ix 提到風，但 B 段只說高樓會 block the breezes，沒有比較不同城市的風速。
questions.quote: Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofing felt absorb most of the sunlight that falls on them and release it slowly as heat after sunset

questions.explain:
答案是 iv。C 段談白色屋頂，好處 is felt chiefly by the people living on the top floor，對街道溫度的影響小得多。
陷阱：iii 提到冷氣費用，但 C 段說的是頂樓住戶的冷氣需求下降，不是冷氣變貴。
questions.quote: The benefit is felt chiefly by the people living on the top floor

questions.explain:
答案是 ii。D 段是洛杉磯把路面漆成淺灰色的實驗：路面確實變涼了，但反射的陽光從下方照到行人，人反而覺得更熱。
同義轉換：experimented with ＝ an experiment；could actually feel hotter than before ＝ unintended consequences。
questions.quote: a person standing on the road at midday could actually feel hotter than before

questions.explain:
答案是 viii。E 段先肯定樹的效果，接著用兩個短句點出兩個問題：But trees are slow 和 Trees are also unevenly shared。
同義轉換：slow ＝ a slow remedy；unevenly shared ＝ not shared equally。

答案是 v。F 段談 Ahmedabad 的計畫（預警醫院、開放公共建築、調整工時），結論是誰在高溫中受害，取決於城市怎麼被組織，不只是怎麼被建造。
同義轉換：how that city is organised ＝ organisation；how it is built ＝ construction。
questions.quote: Who suffers in a hot city depends as much on how that city is organised as on how it is built.

questions.explain:
答案是 B（淺色路面）。陽光從淺色路面反射，從下方照到行人，站在路上的人 could actually feel hotter than before。
陷阱：路面本身是變涼的（cooler to the touch），變熱的是人的感受，題目問的正是後者。
questions.quote: sunlight bouncing off the pale surface struck pedestrians from below

questions.explain:
答案是 A（白色屋頂）。在寒冷地區，反光屋頂冬天吸收的太陽熱較少，heating bills may rise slightly。
同義轉換：heating bills ＝ energy costs；in winter ＝ at one time of year。
questions.quote: a reflective roof absorbs less of the sun's warmth in winter and heating bills may rise slightly

questions.explain:
答案是 C（種樹）。樹苗可能要二十年才能提供有用的樹蔭，這段期間 it must be watered and protected。
同義轉換：watered and protected ＝ continuing care；twenty years ＝ many years。
questions.quote: A sapling may take twenty years to provide useful shade, and during that time it must be watered and protected

questions.explain:
答案是 B（淺色路面）。塗層 wore away under traffic and needed to be reapplied。
解題關鍵：這題和第 20 題答案相同，指示中的 NB 已經提醒字母可以重複使用。
questions.quote: The coating also wore away under traffic and needed to be reapplied.

questions.explain:
答案是 villages。Luke Howard 把倫敦的溫度紀錄和 villages outside it 的紀錄相比。
陷阱：不要填 countryside。countryside 出現在第一句的一般描述裡，Howard 實際比較的地點是 villages，而且題目的 outside the city 對應 outside it。
questions.quote: compared temperature readings taken in London with those from villages outside it

questions.explain:
答案是 leaves（葉子）。植物 cools the air as water evaporates from leaves。
解題關鍵：題目幾乎照原文，as 換成 when。
questions.quote: which cools the air as water evaporates from leaves

questions.explain:
答案是 hospitals。在這個計畫下 hospitals are warned in advance of dangerous temperatures。
同義轉換：warned in advance ＝ receive early warning。
questions.quote: hospitals are warned in advance of dangerous temperatures
